newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank may report lower 1996 profit - WestLB.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank may report lower 1996 profit - WestLB.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank is likely to report a lower profit for 1996, largely due to a fall in domestic interest rate income, Westdeutsche Landesbank said on Thursday.
The bank, which regularly produces outlook reports on Bundesbank profit, predicted earnings of 9.4 billion marks for this year, down from 10.9 billion in 1995.

The bulk of Bundesbank profits are transferred annually to the Bonn government. Bonn traditionally budgets for income of seven billion marks from the central bank each year and any excess is used to retire old debt.
WestLB said it expected 8.5 billion marks to be transferred to government coffers in 1996.
Continued interest rate cuts were cited as the main factor behind a reduction in domestic interest income to 6.2 billion marks from 8.6 billion in 1995.

WestLB said it expected that the central bank's securities repurchase rate or repo would be on average 1-1/4 percentage points lower in 1996 than a year earlier and the disount rate about one percentage point lower on average.
But it said this would be offset in part by a rise in borrowing volumes, adding that credit institutes were expected to take up about 10 billion marks more on average over the year.
For the first time since 1988, interest income from overseas was expected to exceed domestic interest income, WestLB said, predicting a figure of about 6-1/2 billion marks.

Higher holdings of dollar investments, the firmer dollar and the rise in the value of the ECU against the mark were positive factors in this, WestLB said. But negatives were lower ECU holdings and lower short-term rates for ECU and the dollar.
WestLB said it was hard to assess the size of writedowns on currency reserves and other holdings of foreign currencies.

This position in the balance sheet incorporates changes in the book value of holdings as well as profits or losses from the sale or purchase of foreign currencies and changes in foreign claims which could affect reserve holdings.

WestLB said it seemed unlikely that the Bundesbank would have to make writedowns on its currency holdings. Its dollar reserves were already booked at the all-time fixing low of 1.3620 marks and the dollar looked unlikely to fall below this.
But it was likely that further writedowns on its dollar bond holdings would be necessary, WestLB said.
In total, the bank estimated writedowns of 500 million marks for the year.
Interest rate payments abroad were expected to decrease to 500 million marks from 700 million and little change was expected in admistrative and other costs.
A larger transfer to reserves was likely due to an increase in cash in circulation, WestLB said, estimating this at about 800 million marks, up from 600 million in 1995.
